title: Ground-Source ROI Estimator
description: The learner will judge (Bloom Level 5, Evaluate) whether a buried earth-tube air intake is a sound investment for a stated Minnesota house by comparing its yearly heating and cooling savings with its installed cost, and will determine the pipe length that gives the shortest simple payback.
creator: The Science of the Built Environment
author: Dan McCreary
subject: The Science of the Built Environment
chapter_title: Appendix E: Geothermal Heating and Earth-Coupled Air

prerequisites: Appendix E ground temperature model and damping depth
Appendix A energy prices, therms, kilowatt-hours, and COP
Chapter 14 ventilation heat load, 1.08 x cfm x temperature difference

pedagogical.learningObjective: Judge whether a buried earth-tube air intake is a sound investment for a stated Minnesota house, and determine the pipe length that gives the shortest simple payback.
recommendedUsage: Read the chart at the starting settings of 200 ft of pipe, $40 per foot, a $2,000 fixed cost, and a 95 percent gas furnace. The left bar of each month is the home with the standard intake and the right bar is the home with the ground-source intake.
Hover over a month, or press Show table, to read the outdoor temperature, the soil temperature at 8 ft, the intake air temperature, and the dollars saved.
Drag the pipe length slider from 50 ft to 400 ft and watch the tiles: the yearly savings level off while the installed cost keeps rising.
Answer the challenge by typing the pipe length that pays back fastest, then change the fixed cost, the cost per foot, and the heating system and answer again.
activities: Predict (5 min): Students write down whether doubling the pipe from 200 ft to 400 ft will double the yearly savings, then test the prediction.
Reproduce (10 min): Students check the January row of the table by hand against the Appendix E worked example.
Optimize (10 min): Students find the pipe length with the shortest payback at $20, $40, and $80 per foot and explain why the best length gets shorter as the trench gets more expensive.
Evaluate (10 min): Students compare the three heating systems and write a recommendation for a homeowner, stating the payback, the 30-year return, and two things the model leaves out.
assessment: Students calculate the installed cost, simple payback, and 30-year ROI for a system that costs $5,600 and saves $82 a year, showing each step.
Students explain why the ground source saves nothing in April even though the soil is at a steady temperature.
misconceptions: Doubling the pipe length doubles the savings.
Heat from the ground is free, so the payback must be short.
The ground helps in every month.
The saving depends only on the pipe, not on what the saved heat would have cost.
